feature.title: Blacksmiths, broom-makers and a fiddle band at Marble Springs
feature.deck: The governor's farm throws its founder a birthday party once a year, and the whole thing is free. Saturday it turns 281, with working craftspeople on the grounds from eleven to four.

body.text: John Sevier was born in 1745, which makes Saturday his 281st birthday, and the farm he lived on is still standing at the far south end of the county. Marble Springs has thrown him a party every September for years. It costs nothing to walk in, it runs from eleven to four, and the reason to go is the people working: a blacksmith at a live forge, a cook over an open hearth, someone tying a broom by hand, a weaver at a loom, a potter at a wheel.
What's actually happening on the grounds

These are demonstrations, not a museum case — the craftspeople work through the day and will talk while they do it, and the hands-on crafts are open to all ages. It is the rare local event where a nine-year-old and a sixty-year-old get roughly the same thing out of standing at the same table.

body.text: Getting there, and the heat

Marble Springs sits on West Governor John Sevier Highway, past the Urban Wilderness and well south of the Sevier Avenue end of things — it is a drive, not a walk, from the rest of this week's list. Saturday's forecast is mostly sunny and around 94 degrees. A forge on a 94-degree afternoon is exactly as warm as it sounds, so go early, bring water, and plan on the shade being wherever the trees are rather than wherever you are.
One scheduling note worth having: this is the daytime half of a very full Saturday in South Knoxville. The site closes at four, which leaves the evening open.

stories.imageCaption: Fire and silks on the Visitor Center lawn
stories.title: The Circus Under the Moon returns to the Ijams Park lawn
stories.deck: Aerialists, jugglers and fire performers take the lawn outside the Visitor Center after dark on Saturday — one night, one show, and the only circus in town that ends with the woods behind it.

facts.label: When
facts.value: Sat Sep 19 · gate and marketplace 6 PM · show 7:30–9 PM

facts.label: Where
facts.value: Visitor Center lawn, Ijams Park · 2915 Island Home Ave

facts.label: Tickets
facts.value: $22 adults · $15 kids 6–12 · under 6 free · parking included

facts.label: Intermission
facts.value: Around 8:30

facts.label: Bring
facts.value: A lawn chair or a blanket — the lawn is the seating

facts.label: Food & drink
facts.value: Food trucks and the Ijams beer garden on site

facts.label: Sunset
facts.value: About 7:37, so the fire acts land in real dark

body.text: A troupe of local and regional performers sets up on the grass outside the Ijams Park Visitor Center on Saturday evening, and for ninety minutes the lawn is a circus: acrobats, aerials and silks, jugglers, and the fire performers the park bills as the reason to stay to the end. The gate and the marketplace open at six; the show starts at 7:30 and runs to nine with an intermission around 8:30.
How the night is built

The hour and a half before the show is the part people underuse. The marketplace is open from six, the food trucks are parked, and the Ijams beer garden is pouring — so the sensible version of Saturday is to arrive at six, eat on the grass, and be settled when the light goes. Sunset is about 7:37, which means the show starts in dusk and finishes in full dark. That is deliberate, and it is why the fire acts are back half.
The practical part

Twenty-two dollars for an adult, fifteen for a kid six to twelve, free under six, and parking is included in the ticket — worth knowing, because parking at Ijams Park otherwise costs five dollars a car. There are no seats: bring a lawn chair or a blanket. And the one conflict to plan around is that Tennessee kicks off at Neyland at 7:45 the same night, fifteen minutes after the circus starts. The two audiences are mostly different people, but the bridges are not.

body.text: Ijams Park and Central Cinema have been running Movies Under the Stars on the Visitor Center lawn since May, and Friday is the big one: Lord of the Rings, outdoors, on a screen, with the actual woods sitting right there behind it. The gate opens at seven and the movie starts when it gets dark, which the park puts at about 8:15.
What to expect on the lawn

Twelve dollars a head, with a discount for Ijams and Central Cinema members. Food trucks and the beer garden handle dinner and drinks — no coolers and no outside alcohol, which the park is direct about. Bring a chair or a blanket. Dogs are allowed and have to be leashed the whole time, and on a Friday night with a crowd that is a rule worth taking seriously.
Two left after this

The series has one more date after Friday — Carrie on October 2, which tells you where the calendar is heading. Buy ahead if you can; the park does not promise walk-up tickets. Friday's forecast is mostly sunny and around 94 with a slight chance of an evening storm, so check the event page before you load the car.

stories.title: A 7:45 night kickoff puts the stadium crowd on our side of the river
stories.deck: Tennessee hosts Kennesaw State on Saturday night, and a late kickoff means the South Knoxville parking hunt starts in the afternoon and the walk back across the bridge happens near midnight.

body.text: Tennessee plays Kennesaw State on Saturday at 7:45 on SEC Network — the first night game at Neyland this season, and the last one before conference play starts. None of that is South Knoxville news by itself. What is South Knoxville news is that a 7:45 kickoff moves the whole rhythm of the day: cars start hunting for spaces on this side of the river by mid-afternoon, and the walk back over the bridge happens somewhere around eleven.
Where the spaces actually are

The City counts more than 600 public parking spaces near the Sevier Avenue corridor. More than 200 of those are at Suttree Landing Park and on the streets around it. Another 300-plus are in the Regal garage, which is open to the public on weekends and after six on weekdays. From any of them it is a five-to-ten-minute walk to the Sevier Avenue businesses, and a longer one to the stadium.
If you live here and you are not going

The roundabout construction at Sevier, Foggy Bottom and Island Home is still in the ground, so the corridor is narrower than it looks on a map. Marked pedestrian paths skirt the work. If Saturday night is a stay-home night, it is a good one to walk rather than drive. And if you were planning on the circus at Ijams Park, note that it starts fifteen minutes before kickoff — the lawn is fine, the bridges are the problem.

body.text: Storytime at the Ijams Nature Playscape runs every Saturday morning from ten to noon and costs nothing: somebody reads a book out loud on the blankets, and then it is a craft or it is the climbing logs and the creek. This Saturday the reader is the author. Mona Martin Batchelor will read from "Nora T and the Champion Tree," a children's book of hers that has not been published yet.
Why the Playscape is the right room for it

The Playscape is five acres of deliberately unfinished woods at the Grayson Subaru Preserve — dirt to dig, logs to climb, a creek to stand in. A book about a champion tree read out loud under actual trees is the kind of thing that only works in a place like this, and it is free, which means a family can show up on a whim and leave when the two-year-old is done.
It is a short walk from the Mead's Quarry gravel lot. Saturday will be hot — mostly sunny and around 94 — but the ten-to-noon window is the cool half of that, and the Playscape is shaded.

body.text: Earl's sits at 610 Waterfront Drive, down where Suttree Landing meets the river, and it runs a different special every day of the week. Thursday is ten-dollar Patrón mango margaritas. Friday is nine-dollar spicy pineapple ones. Saturday is eight-dollar house margaritas, and Sunday is seven-dollar mimosas and Bloody Marys. All of them run the full day, eleven to ten.
The new column

What is new this week is a second Saturday board that runs alongside the margaritas: two dollars off drafts and two off pizza, six-dollar Orange Bliss, and beer buckets at six for the price of five, plus a run of four- and five-dollar shots. It is there because the Vols are home at 7:45, and because the tables at Earl's face open water about ten minutes' walk from where half the stadium crowd parks.

The food is the reason to get there before the drinks are, and eleven in the morning is a real opening time rather than a technicality. If Saturday night belongs to the stadium, Sunday at the water is the recovery.
